title: Introduction to Networks
subtitle: Climb the money ladder — one networking question per grade level

questions.q: Which of the following best describes what an IP address does on a network?
options: It speeds up your internet connection
It uniquely identifies a device on a network
It stores files shared between computers
It encrypts data sent over Wi-Fi
questions.note: An IP address is a logical label assigned to every networked device so other devices can locate and communicate with it. This is foundational to all networking.

explain.correct: An IP address (e.g., 192.168.1.10) is a unique logical identifier assigned to each device on a network, allowing routers and switches to deliver packets to the correct destination.
wrong: IP addresses do not affect connection speed — bandwidth and latency are governed by the physical link and ISP plan.
File storage is handled by file servers or shared drives, not IP addressing.
Encryption is provided by protocols like WPA2/WPA3 or TLS, not by an IP address.

questions.q: When you type a website address into your browser and it loads over an encrypted (HTTPS) connection, which port number is used by default?
questions.note: HTTPS uses TCP port 443; plain HTTP uses port 80. Port 22 is SSH and port 25 is SMTP. These are well-known ports defined in the 0–1023 range.

explain.correct: HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) defaults to TCP port 443, which carries TLS-encrypted web traffic between your browser and the web server.
wrong: Port 80 is the default for plain, unencrypted HTTP — not HTTPS.
Port 22 is reserved for SSH (Secure Shell), which provides remote command-line access to servers.
Port 25 is SMTP, used for sending email between mail servers, not for web browsing.

questions.q: A switch receives a frame destined for a device on the SAME local network. How does it decide which port to send the frame out of?
options: It broadcasts the frame out every port simultaneously
It looks up the destination IP address in its routing table
It looks up the destination MAC address in its MAC address table
It asks the router which port to use
questions.note: Switches operate at Layer 2 and forward frames based on MAC addresses stored in a dynamically learned MAC address table (CAM table). Hubs broadcast; routers use IP.

explain.correct: A switch maintains a MAC address table (CAM table) that maps each device's MAC address to the port it was learned on. It forwards the frame only to the port associated with the destination MAC address.
wrong: Broadcasting out every port is what a hub does — or what a switch does only when the destination MAC is unknown (flooding). Once the MAC is learned, it forwards selectively.
Routing tables use IP addresses and are the job of a router (Layer 3), not a switch (Layer 2).
Switches make their own forwarding decisions from their MAC table; they do not consult a router for local traffic.

questions.q: What is an SSID on a wireless network?
options: The unique hardware address burned into your wireless adapter
The human-readable name that identifies a wireless network
The encryption key used to secure the Wi-Fi signal
The channel number assigned to avoid interference
questions.note: SSID stands for Service Set Identifier — the broadcast name of the wireless network (e.g., 'HomeNetwork'). It is separate from authentication credentials and the radio channel.

explain.correct: The SSID (Service Set Identifier) is the human-readable name of a wireless network, such as 'CoffeeShop_WiFi'. Devices scan for and connect to a network by its SSID.
wrong: The unique hardware address burned into a network adapter is the MAC address (Media Access Control), not an SSID.
The encryption key (passphrase) is the WPA2/WPA3 pre-shared key used to authenticate and encrypt the connection — not the SSID.
The radio channel (e.g., channel 1, 6, or 11 on 2.4 GHz) is a separate setting on the access point; it is not the SSID.

questions.q: A video-streaming app sends data with no retransmission of lost packets, prioritizing continuous playback over perfect accuracy. Which transport protocol is it most likely using?
options: TCP, because it guarantees delivery
UDP, because it is connectionless and does not retransmit lost data
ICMP, because it checks for path reachability
HTTP, because websites use it for media delivery
questions.note: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and fire-and-forget — ideal for real-time media where a dropped frame is preferable to a stall caused by waiting for retransmission.

explain.correct: UDP is connectionless and does not perform retransmission or sequencing. A dropped packet simply produces a brief glitch, which is acceptable in live video or VoIP where timeliness matters more than perfection.
wrong: TCP uses a three-way handshake and retransmits every lost segment, which introduces latency — undesirable for real-time streaming.
ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is used for diagnostic messages like ping; it is not a transport protocol for streaming data.
HTTP is an application-layer protocol that rides on top of TCP — it is not a transport protocol itself, and it inherits TCP's retransmission overhead.

questions.q: A PC has IP 192.168.10.50, subnet mask 255.255.255.0, and default gateway 192.168.10.1. It tries to reach 8.8.8.8 (Google DNS). What does the PC send the packet to first?
options: Directly to 8.8.8.8, because it knows the IP address
Its default gateway at 192.168.10.1, because 8.8.8.8 is outside its subnet
The DNS server, because it must resolve the IP before sending
The subnet broadcast address 192.168.10.255
questions.note: With a /24 mask (255.255.255.0) the PC's network is 192.168.10.0. Any destination outside that range is off-subnet, so the PC forwards the packet to its default gateway (the router's LAN interface).

explain.correct: The subnet mask 255.255.255.0 (/24) means the PC's local network is 192.168.10.0–192.168.10.254. Because 8.8.8.8 is not in that range, the PC marks it as remote and sends the packet to its default gateway (192.168.10.1), which is the router's LAN-side IP address.
wrong: A PC cannot send a packet directly to a remote host — it has no route to reach it directly. All off-subnet traffic must go through the default gateway.
DNS resolution translates a domain name (like google.com) to an IP address. Here the IP is already known (8.8.8.8), so DNS is not involved in this step.
The broadcast address (192.168.10.255) is used to reach all hosts on the local subnet simultaneously, not to forward traffic to a remote destination.

questions.q: A technician runs `tracert 8.8.8.8` and sees 12 hops before reaching the destination. What does each hop in the tracert output represent?
options: A DNS server that resolved part of the address
A router or Layer 3 device that forwarded the packet along the path
A switch that forwarded the frame at Layer 2
A firewall that inspected and allowed the packet
questions.note: Tracert/traceroute uses incrementing TTL values; each router that decrements TTL to 0 sends an ICMP Time Exceeded reply, revealing itself as a hop. Switches are invisible because they operate at Layer 2.

explain.correct: Tracert works by sending packets with increasing TTL (Time To Live) values starting at 1. Each router that receives a packet decrements the TTL; when it hits 0 the router returns an ICMP Time Exceeded message, revealing its IP address as a 'hop' on the path.
wrong: DNS servers translate names to IP addresses but are not normally visible as hops in a tracert path unless DNS traffic specifically routes through them.
Switches operate at Layer 2 (MAC addresses) and are transparent to IP-level tools like tracert; they do not decrement TTL and do not appear as hops.
Firewalls may be present along the path but they appear as routable hops only if they forward the packet and decrement TTL; many silently drop ICMP probes and appear as '* * *' timeouts.

questions.q: In the OSI model, at which layer does a router operate, and what addressing does it use to make forwarding decisions?
options: Layer 1 (Physical) — it uses electrical signals
Layer 2 (Data Link) — it uses MAC addresses
Layer 3 (Network) — it uses IP addresses
Layer 4 (Transport) — it uses port numbers
questions.note: Routers are Layer 3 (Network layer) devices that read IP headers to determine the best path to a destination network. Switches are Layer 2; hubs are Layer 1.

explain.correct: Routers operate at OSI Layer 3 (the Network layer). They examine the destination IP address in the IP header, consult their routing table, and forward the packet toward the destination network.
wrong: Layer 1 (Physical) covers the raw electrical, optical, or radio signals. Hubs are the classic Layer 1 device — they simply repeat signals to all ports with no address awareness.
Layer 2 (Data Link) uses MAC addresses for local delivery within the same network segment. Switches are Layer 2 devices that learn MAC addresses and forward frames accordingly.

Layer 4 (Transport) uses port numbers to identify applications and services (e.g., TCP 80 for HTTP). Firewalls and load balancers can inspect Layer 4 headers, but a standard router forwards at Layer 3.

questions.q: A home router uses NAT/PAT to allow 50 devices on the 192.168.1.0/24 network to share a single public IP. How does the router track which reply packet belongs to which internal device?
options: It assigns each device a unique public IP address from a pool
It stores the device's MAC address in each outbound packet header
It records the internal IP + port number mapped to a unique source port number on the public IP, in a NAT translation table
It uses DHCP lease records to route replies back to each device
questions.note: PAT (Port Address Translation) overloads a single public IP by tracking unique source port numbers per internal session in the NAT table, allowing thousands of simultaneous connections from one public address.

explain.correct: With PAT (a form of NAT), the router rewrites outbound packets so they all appear to come from the single public IP but with a unique source port per session. The NAT translation table records the mapping of (internal IP : internal port) to (public IP : translated port). When a reply arrives, the router looks up the translated port to identify the correct internal host and port to forward it to.
wrong: Assigning each device a unique public IP would be traditional one-to-one NAT, which would require 50 public IPs — defeating the entire purpose of NAT/PAT.
MAC addresses are Layer 2 constructs that do not travel beyond the local network segment and are never included in routed IP packets.
DHCP lease records map IP addresses to MAC addresses for allocation purposes; the router does not use DHCP records to route individual reply packets back to internal hosts.

questions.q: A network admin is securing a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network (which offers only 3 non-overlapping channels: 1, 6, and 11). Which is the CURRENT wireless security standard — the one that replaced WPA2 and uses the SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) handshake?
options: WEP
WPA
WPA2-PSK
WPA3
questions.note: WPA3 is the current Wi-Fi security standard; it replaced WPA2's Pre-Shared Key 4-way handshake with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which resists offline dictionary attacks. On 2.4 GHz, only channels 1, 6, and 11 are non-overlapping.

explain.correct: WPA3 is the current standard; its SAE handshake gives a stronger, dictionary-attack-resistant key exchange, replacing WPA2-PSK.
wrong: WEP (RC4) is obsolete and was cracked years ago — never use it.
WPA (TKIP) was a stopgap after WEP and is now deprecated.
WPA2-PSK (AES) was the prior standard, but its 4-way handshake is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks; WPA3/SAE replaced it.

questions.q: A workstation boots and sends a broadcast to obtain network configuration automatically. In the correct order of the DHCP DORA process, what is the SECOND message exchanged, and who sends it?
options: Discover — sent by the client as a broadcast to find available DHCP servers
Offer — sent by the DHCP server in response to the Discover, proposing an IP address
Request — sent by the client to formally request the offered IP address
Acknowledge — sent by the DHCP server to confirm the lease and deliver the full configuration
questions.note: DHCP DORA: (1) Discover (client broadcast), (2) Offer (server unicast/broadcast with proposed IP), (3) Request (client broadcasts acceptance), (4) Acknowledge (server confirms lease with IP, mask, gateway, DNS). The Offer is the second message and comes from the server.

explain.correct: In the DHCP DORA handshake, the second message is the Offer (O), sent by the DHCP server. After receiving the client's broadcast Discover, the server responds with a DHCPOFFER containing a proposed IP address, the subnet mask, default gateway, DNS server address, and lease duration.
wrong: The Discover (D) is the FIRST message — a broadcast sent by the client (using source IP 0.0.0.0, destination 255.255.255.255) because it has no IP address yet and doesn't know where the DHCP server is.
The Request (R) is the THIRD message — after the client receives one or more Offers, it broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST to formally accept one offer and inform other servers that their offers were declined.
The Acknowledge (A) is the FOURTH and final message — the DHCP server confirms the lease by sending a DHCPACK containing the full configuration parameters (IP, mask, gateway, DNS, lease time).
